source: Jones & Steinhardt (2022) Capturing Failures of Large Language Models via Human Cognitive Biases
finding: First paper to use human cognitive biases as hypotheses for code-model failures. Irrelevant preceding functions with a framing line (e.g. pass, assert False) cut Codex accuracy and the line was copied into the output.
numbers: HumanEval 164 problems. Codex baseline accuracy 32.9%, CodeGen 25.6%. With framing, accuracy fell by 22.3 to 30.5 points for Codex. Framing line appeared in output 81% (Codex) and 70.7% (CodeGen) of the time vs 4.5% and 0.0% on untransformed prompts. Even return False, which contradicts the signature, was copied 65.6% (Codex).
quote: code generation models may adjust their output towards related solutions, when these solutions are included in the prompt
limits: Pre-ChatGPT models (Codex, CodeGen). Hypothesis-driven probe, no human control group. Framing here is really irrelevant-context sensitivity.
agent_relevance: Context in the prompt is not neutral: an agent that carries stale or wrong snippets in its context will copy them. Supports clean-context retries.

source: Jones & Steinhardt (2022) Capturing Failures of Large Language Models via Human Cognitive Biases
finding: Anchoring test: prepend a near-correct but wrong 'anchor function' (print-var or add-var lines). Accuracy dropped and anchor lines showed up in outputs, including inside correct solutions.
numbers: Print-var: Codex wrote the anchor for-loop in 32-61% of solutions and print(var) in 26-44%, depending on how many canonical solution lines were given. Anchor lines also in 3-11% (loop) and 1-9% (print) of correct solutions. Add-var: 'return tmp' in 26-46% (Codex), 13-79% (CodeGen). Verbatim copy only 7-12% (Codex), 4-12% (CodeGen). Renaming the anchor function changed results negligibly.
limits: Anchoring here means copying a prior wrong draft, not numeric-estimate anchoring. Only HumanEval. CodeGen gave noisy output on other prompt sets.
agent_relevance: An agent's own first failed attempt is an anchor for its second. Re-deriving from the spec, not editing the failed draft, is the countermeasure.

source: Jones & Steinhardt (2022) Capturing Failures of Large Language Models via Human Cognitive Biases
finding: Availability heuristic test: flipping unary-then-binary to binary-then-unary operation order broke Codex, and it mostly output the more frequent order. Attribute substitution test: a conflicting function name overrode the docstring.
numbers: Availability: 12 op combinations, Codex accuracy 50% -> 17% on flipped order; 75% of errors were the unary-first (frequent) solution. Attribute substitution: 90 MathEquation prompts; correct only 4.4-4.6% once a conflicting name was given, output matched the function name 80.0% (name in docstring), 70.0% (in signature), 51.7% (name first). Without the name: 100% correct.
limits: Codex only for these two (CodeGen gave nonsense on these prompts). Small synthetic prompt set.
agent_relevance: Frequent patterns beat the stated spec. Tests for the agent should include inputs where the common pattern is wrong (mutated spec), as G3 asks.

source: Suri et al. (2023) Do Large Language Models Show Decision Heuristics Similar to Humans? A Case Study Using GPT-3.5
finding: GPT-3.5 shows human-like anchoring: estimates track a random anchor, with a size close to a matched human sample.
numbers: Anchoring study (books in a house). Low anchor (10-20): ChatGPT mean 20.83 (SE 3.38), humans 22.50. High anchor (100-200): ChatGPT 105.97 (SE 9.08), humans 80.50. ChatGPT low vs high t(58)=8.78, p<.0001; humans t(58)=5.55. ChatGPT vs humans, high anchor: t(58)=1.90, p=.06. GPT-4: low 22.0, high 94.33 (5 trials each).
quote: language may play a role in generating these effects in humans
limits: Small trial counts (GPT-4 only 5 per condition). Humans were online workers, 60 people. Estimation task, not software.
agent_relevance: Numeric anchors in a prompt (a deadline, a prior estimate, a suggested value) will pull the agent's estimates; do not show the agent a number before it forms its own.

source: Suri et al. (2023) Decision Heuristics in GPT-3.5, framing study
finding: Framing, representativeness/availability and endowment effects were also found in GPT-3.5, matching humans in direction.
numbers: Framing: all 11 positive-frame trials rated efficacy 5 (1-7 scale), all 11 negative-frame trials rated 4. Humans 5.2 vs 4.6, t(80)=3.86, p<.001.
limits: Four small studies. Direction matches humans but the model has no loss aversion or effort reduction, so the cause is likely language statistics.
agent_relevance: Supports the idea that biases come from text patterns, so a scaffold can counter them with text (instructions), not only training.

source: Comprehensive Evaluation of Cognitive Biases in LLMs (2024, v2 Oct 2025)
finding: Large benchmark: 30 cognitive biases in 20 LLMs from 8 developers. All models were significantly biased on at least some biases; most were positive, as in humans.
numbers: 30,000 test cases (200 scenarios x 30 biases). Score is signed; random baseline about 0. Mean over all 30 biases per model ranged 0.03 (Llama 3.2 1B) to 0.22 (Phi-3.5).
limits: Decision-scenario text templates, not code tasks. Scores depend on the authors' test design. Model size and Arena score did not clearly predict bias. Column-to-model mapping read from figure text.
agent_relevance: Bias is not removed by capability. Plan guardrails assuming a strong model is still biased.

source: Comprehensive Evaluation of Cognitive Biases in LLMs (2024, v2 Oct 2025)
finding: Anchoring is one of the strongest biases in LLMs; confirmation bias is weak on average but very uneven by model.
numbers: Anchoring mean score 0.39 (GPT-4o 0.60, GPT-4o mini 0.40, GPT-3.5 0.35, Llama 3.1 70B 0.64, Llama 3.2 1B 0.15). Confirmation bias mean 0.15: GPT-4o 0.00, GPT-3.5 0.09, Llama 3.1 70B 0.69, Gemma 2 27B 0.69, Gemma 2 9B 0.72, Gemini 1.5 Pro 0.09.
limits: Heatmap values read from the figure text. Confirmation-bias test is a decision scenario, not hypothesis testing.
agent_relevance: Anchoring is the robust failure, confirmation depends on the model. Check per model, do not assume.

source: Comprehensive Evaluation of Cognitive Biases in LLMs (2024, v2 Oct 2025)
finding: Optimism-related and planning biases are weak in LLMs; software-related biases (escalation of commitment, not invented here) are also small.
numbers: Mean scores: Optimism Bias 0.06, Planning Fallacy -0.02 (slightly negative), Escalation of Commitment 0.07, Not Invented Here 0.08, Availability Heuristic 0.11, Framing 0.41, Halo 0.34, Hindsight 0.33, Information Bias 0.54, Status-quo -0.42, Disposition Effect -0.69.
limits: Hypothetical scenarios; models may be recognising a known bias quiz. Negative scores mean preference for change.
agent_relevance: Do not spend schema space on optimism or planning fallacy for the model itself. Spend it on anchoring, framing and information-seeking.

source: Cognitive Biases in LLM-Assisted Software Development (2026, ICSE)
finding: Observation of 14 developers (7 student, 7 professional) using LLM assistants: nearly half of all actions showed a cognitive bias, more when the action involved the LLM. New taxonomy of 90 biases in 15 categories.
numbers: 2,013 actions, 808 (40.2%) with LLM. Biased actions 983/2013 (48.8%); LLM actions with a bias 456/808 (56.4%); chi-square LLM vs bias chi2(1,N=2013)=30.72, p=2.97e-8. Prior human-only study: 45.72% of 2,084 actions. Reversals 25% overall, 29.5% of LLM actions.
limits: Small sample, one 60-minute session each. Biases coded by authors. Survey n=22. No tested mitigation.
agent_relevance: Human-side biases when working with an LLM. A scaffold agent may inherit the human's anchors through the prompt, so treat user-supplied guesses as claims.

source: Cognitive Biases in LLM-Assisted Software Development (2026), category table
finding: Which biases hit LLM actions most: instant gratification, suggester preference, familiarity preference. Belief confirmation and fixation (which includes anchoring) lead to reversals often.
numbers: LLM actions by category: Instant Gratification 156 (29.5% reversed), Suggester Preference 102 (21.5%), Familiarity 89 (28%), Memory bias 80 (32.5%), Belief Confirmation 77 (33.8%), Fixation (incl. anchoring) 76 (43.4%), Optimism/Pessimism 41 (36.6%). Only Fixation (chi2=7.15, p=.0075) and Familiarity (chi2=11.87, p=.0006) were significantly tied to reversal within LLM actions.
limits: No separate count for confirmation or anchoring alone. Bias-reversal link overall p=0.058, not significant after correction. Last 27k characters of the page not read.
agent_relevance: Fixation on the first LLM suggestion is the costly one. Schema should force a second independent candidate before testing (S4 harvest).

source: Failing to Falsify: Evaluating and Mitigating Confirmation Bias in Language Models (2026)
finding: Wason 2-4-6 style rule discovery across 11 model settings: models mostly propose tests that confirm their hypothesis. Lower bias goes with higher success.
numbers: Success 6% to 78% within a 45-turn cap. Thinking-mode baseline success / ratio of infirming to confirming tests (I:C): Qwen3-8B 0.21/0.15, Qwen3-32B 0.41/0.14, QwQ-32B 0.50/0.36, Gemini-2.5-Pro 0.73/0.66. Non-thinking: GPT-4o 0.11/0.25, Qwen3-8B 0.06/0.35. Human reference: correct first-announcers had I:C 1.79 vs 0.24 for incorrect ones.
quote: LLMs often propose triples to confirm their hypothesis rather than trying to falsify it
limits: Abstract rule task, not code. Gains significant for thinking models, mixed for non-thinking. Last 36k characters of the page not read.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G3: left alone, models test to confirm. Falsifying tests must be forced by the schema.

source: Failing to Falsify (2026), prompt interventions
finding: Two human-derived prompts reduce confirmation bias: Think-in-Opposites and Dual-Goal.
numbers: Average success rose from 42% to 56%. Think-in-Opposites raised success in all 11 settings; Dual-Goal in 8 of 11; I:C ratio rose in 18 of 22 cases. Qwen3-32B thinking: baseline 0.41 / TiO 0.61 / Dual-Goal 0.60; I:C 0.14 -> 0.54 / 0.77. QwQ-32B 0.50 -> 0.59 / 0.58, I:C 0.36 -> 0.37 / 0.81.
limits: Gains clearest in reasoning models. Prompts raise I:C but success does not rise as much, so more falsifying tests is not the whole story.
agent_relevance: A prompt-only fix that works in an agent loop: ask for a test that would break the hypothesis and also one that would confirm it.

source: Failing to Falsify (2026), distillation
finding: Distilling the intervention into weights removes the need for the prompt and partly transfers to a different task (Blicket).
numbers: Wason: Qwen3-8B 0.21 -> 0.35 (own TiO) -> 0.59 (32B teacher with TiO); Qwen3-32B 0.41 -> 0.64 with 32B TiO. Blicket: Qwen3-32B 0.57 -> 0.77, I:C 0.54 -> 0.88. Intervention prompts still beat distillation on Blicket.
limits: Weights training, so not available to our scaffold. Transfer shown on one extra task only.
agent_relevance: Shows the behaviour is learnable; for us, the prompt version is the usable part.

source: FalsifyBench: generalised 2-4-6 on semantic properties (2026)
finding: Twelve models played 100 hidden-property games (20 turns). Models that ask negative tests (outside the current hypothesis) win far more. Instruction-tuned models mostly test positives.
numbers: 12 models x 100 games = 1,200 observations. Success: GPT-5.2-Chat 75%, GPT-OSS-120B 68%, DeepSeek-V3.1 41%, other instruction-tuned 33-35%, Qwen3.5-9B 21%, GPT-5-Nano 12%. Positive-test share: GPT-5.2-Chat 27.3%, GPT-OSS-20B 24.2%, GPT-5-Mini 39.0%, instruction-tuned 66-82%. Success vs positive-test rate Spearman rho=-0.779, p=.003. Conclusive falsification rate vs positive rate rho=-0.937.
limits: No falsification-prompt intervention tested in this paper. Semantic category games, not code. Oracle errors had no credible effect.
agent_relevance: Strongest numeric support that falsifying probes drive success; reasoning models already do it more.

source: WILT: multi-turn, memorization-robust inductive logic benchmark (2024)
finding: WILT, a 2-4-6 inspired benchmark: hidden 3-input Python rule, up to 30 tests then one guess. Even the best model solved only 28%. Failure modes include confirmation bias and repeat tests.
numbers: Full split 50 rules: Claude 3.5 Sonnet 14/50 (28%), o1-mini 13 (26%), o1-preview 12 (24%), GPT-4o 9 (18%), Llama 3.1 405B 8 (16%), Gemini 1.5 Pro 5 (10%), GPT-4o-mini 6 (12%), Claude 3 Haiku 1 (2%), Gemma 2 9B 0. Deepseek-v2.5-chat averaged 489 repeated tests.
limits: No human baseline in paper. Failure modes listed by authors, no quantified bias rate. Older models.
agent_relevance: Rule inference with test probes is a code-like task where models fail; use as a smoke test for G3 prompts.

source: Zhao, Zhou, Cohen (2026) Evaluating and Mitigating the Misguidance Effect of Buggy Code in LLM-Generated Unit Tests
finding: Showing the buggy code to the test writer makes it write tests that lock in the bug. Direct LLM version of confirmation bias in testing.
numbers: Defects4J v3.0, 318 focal methods, 233 defects, 11 LLMs. Buggy code input: misguided tests 137.69 per model (3.84%), effective bug-finding tests 104.15 (2.98%). Fixed code input: misguided 16.46 (0.46%), effective 304.08 (8.51%). Misguided tests are only about 6.23% of tests that pass on buggy code. Model-internal scores favour same-wrong-behavior tests on buggy input.
limits: One benchmark (Java, Defects4J). Misguided count correlates with effective count (r=0.90), so the metric partly tracks test volume. Last 28k characters not read.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G3: write tests from the spec, not from the code under test.

source: Zhao, Zhou, Cohen (2026) Misguidance Effect of Buggy Code, mitigation
finding: Mitigation: replace the code with an LLM-written specification docstring before generating tests. More bug-finding tests, fewer misguided ones.
numbers: Docstring only: misguided 113.00 (2.69%), effective 186.77 (4.50%) vs code only 137.69 / 104.15. Advanced docstring prompt: misguided 87.38 (1.91%), effective 230.23 (4.98%). Methods with at least one effective test 45.46 -> 73.31 -> 87.15. Multi-round: effective +35.69 (docstring) vs +17.62 (code). Cost: hallucinated-behavior tests 18.15% vs 16.36%; 15.09% (Gemini) and 20.75% (Qwen) docstrings kept the original bug; correct behavior recovered in 62.26% / 47.48%.
limits: Spec is itself generated from the buggy code, so it can inherit the bug. Compile failure rate about 20% both ways.
agent_relevance: Concrete operator: generate tests from a spec produced without looking at the candidate code (S4 TEST).

source: BlindSpotEval / ObligBench: blind spots in LLM-generated unit tests (2026)
finding: LLM-written tests cluster on normal inputs and happy paths. Edge and exception paths are rarely checked.
numbers: 14,320 tests from 4 LLMs and 4 prompting strategies on 895 complex + 700 simple Java functions. Unusual-argument coverage: null 34.8%, negative 23.8%, empty 38.8% vs booleans above 93%. Catch-block adequacy 0.100, default-branch 0.312. 15.6% of failures came from incorrect assertions.
limits: Abstract only read. Java only.
agent_relevance: Matches the human positive-test habit: models also test to pass. Ask explicitly for boundary and failure cases.

source: Olausson, Inala, Wang, Gao, Solar-Lezama (2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation?
finding: Self-repair gains are small once compute is matched. The bottleneck is the model's feedback about its own code.
numbers: CodeLlama-13b, GPT-3.5, GPT-4 on HumanEval and APPS. Normalized pass rate (repair vs same-budget resampling) often 0.92-1.06, i.e. no gain. Repair success with GPT-4 explanations 33.30% overall (42.64% intro, 19.33% interview, 3.67% competition) vs human feedback 52.60% (62.21%, 45.67%, 14.67%).
limits: Python, self-contained tasks. Human feedback study small.
agent_relevance: Keep repair loops short; spend budget on fresh candidates plus an independent check.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Without an external signal, asking the model to review its answer does not help and often hurts. With oracle labels it helps a lot, so the gain comes from the outside check, not from reconsidering.
numbers: GPT-3.5 intrinsic: CommonSenseQA 75.8 -> 38.1 (round 1) -> 41.8; GSM8K 75.9 -> 75.1 -> 74.7. GPT-4: GSM8K 95.5 -> 91.5 -> 89.0; CommonSenseQA 82.0 -> 79.5 -> 80.0; HotpotQA 49.0 -> 49.0 -> 43.0. Oracle labels: GPT-4 GSM8K 97.5, HotpotQA 59.0 (from 49.0).
limits: Reasoning QA, not code. Oracle use is unrealistic.
agent_relevance: Reinforces G3: a pass has to come from something the answer was not fitted to; self-review is not such a check.

source: Sharma et al. (2023) Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models
finding: Five assistants consistently agree with a user's stated view; humans and preference models sometimes prefer sycophantic answers over correct ones.
numbers: Five assistants, four free-form tasks. No percentages on the abstract page.
limits: Abstract only read.
agent_relevance: A user's guess about the bug is a confirmation anchor; the agent should test it, not adopt it.

source: Dasgupta et al. (2022) Language models show human-like content effects on reasoning
finding: On NLI, syllogisms and the Wason selection task, models, like humans, reason better when content agrees with the logic. Content effects mirror belief bias.
numbers: Abstract only: no numbers read.
limits: Abstract only read. The Wason selection task is the classic confirmation-bias logic test.
agent_relevance: Logic training in humans reduced confirmation bias; the model may need the abstract-rule form of the check, not a realistic story.

source: Justice or Prejudice? Quantifying Biases in LLM-as-a-Judge (2024)
finding: 12 biases in LLM judges measured with the CALM framework. Bias persists in specific tasks even in strong models.
numbers: 12 biases; model counts not on the abstract page.
limits: Abstract only read.
agent_relevance: A model used as grader of its own output is a biased check; prefer execution.

source: Tian & Zhang (2024) Selective Prompt Anchoring for Code Generation
finding: A different use of 'anchoring': amplify the spec tokens during decoding because attention to the prompt fades as code grows. Training-free.
numbers: 6 code LLMs, 6 benchmarks. Pass@1 gains up to +12.9 points (DeepSeek-Coder 6.7B HumanEval 75.6 -> 88.5, above unmodified 33B at 81.7). Average +5.5 on HumanEval/MBPP variants; BigCodeBench avg about +1.6, LiveCodeBench about +1.9. Latency about 1.27x. Human-picked tokens did worse (3.66% vs 5.48%).
limits: Needs logit access; no gain on MMLU; fixed strength setting. Name overlap with the bias is only wording.
agent_relevance: Not usable through an API-only scaffold, but suggests restating the spec near the end of a long context.

source: Empirical Study of the Anchoring Effect in LLMs: Existence, Mechanism, and Potential Mitigations (SynAnchors, 2025)
finding: SynAnchors dataset shows anchoring in 22%-61% of questions across 11 LLMs; effect sits in shallow layers; reasoning models are least anchored.
numbers: 100 questions (60 semantic, 40 numeric), each asked 100 times. Share anchored: Qwen3-235B thinking 22.0%, DeepSeek-R1 25.0%, Qwen2.5-0.5B 60.5%. Human A-Index about 0.4-0.6. Causal tracing on Llama-3.1-8B: effect before middle layers.
limits: Non-code questions. Qwen3 used 30 samples. Last 3k characters not read.
agent_relevance: Anchoring is real across scales; reasoning at inference reduces it more than prompts do.

source: SynAnchors (2025), mitigation tests
finding: Conventional fixes barely help; only explicit two-phase reasoning (Anti-DP) gave a meaningful cut.
numbers: Share of questions anchored, Llama-3.1-8B / Qwen2.5-7B, baseline 34.7% / 40.0%: question-aware prompt ('think cautiously') 36.8% / 43.0% (worse); self-improving 38.4% / 48.0% (worse); adversarial finetune 33.3% / 37.0%; DoLa 37.5-38.5% / 38-40%; Anti-DP 24.7% / 40.8%. Best case about 10 points lower, none eliminated.
limits: Small models. Anti-DP gave no overall gain on Qwen.
agent_relevance: Telling the model to 'be careful' fails; structured reasoning that commits to an answer before seeing the anchor is better.
